claims.source: The otx1b and otx2 genes, which are expressed in the anterior neural plate, also showed slightly reduced expression (otx1b, reduced to 81 ± 11% and otx2, 79 ± 10%) suggesting that the anterior neural plate may be slightly reduced in size in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: otx2 expression was reduced to 79 ± 10% of wildtype levels in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: The otx1b and otx2 genes, which are expressed in the anterior neural plate, also showed slightly reduced expression (otx1b, reduced to 81 ± 11% and otx2, 79 ± 10%) suggesting that the anterior neural plate may be slightly reduced in size in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data mentioned in the text and shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: The anterior neural plate may be slightly reduced in size in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: The otx1b and otx2 genes, which are expressed in the anterior neural plate, also showed slightly reduced expression (otx1b, reduced to 81 ± 11% and otx2, 79 ± 10%) suggesting that the anterior neural plate may be slightly reduced in size in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the reduced expression of otx1b and otx2 genes, and supported by data showing the forebrain domain is reduced to 76% of wildtype size (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: A reduction in the size of the prospective forebrain of Ztcf7l1a-/- embryos may contribute to the reduced levels of expression of tcf7l1b, tcf7l2 and otx genes.
claims.source: This indicates that a reduction in the size of the prospective forebrain of Ztcf7l1a-/- embryos may contribute to the reduced levels of expression of tcf7l1b, tcf7l2 and otx genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the forebrain domain is reduced in size and that genes expressed in this domain show reduced expression levels.

claims.claim: RT-qPCR showed very reduced expression of eye field genes in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos.
claims.source: More remarkable than the modest changes in tcf and otx gene expression was the finding that RT-qPCR showed very reduced expression of eye field genes in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos (Figure 2A; rx3 reduced to 26 ± 1%, p=0.0002 and six3b reduced to 44 ± 5%, p=0.0091 of wildtype levels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: rx3 expression was reduced to 26 ± 1% of wildtype levels in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos.
claims.source: More remarkable than the modest changes in tcf and otx gene expression was the finding that RT-qPCR showed very reduced expression of eye field genes in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos (Figure 2A; rx3 reduced to 26 ± 1%, p=0.0002 and six3b reduced to 44 ± 5%, p=0.0091 of wildtype levels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: six3b expression was reduced to 44 ± 5% of wildtype levels in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos.
claims.source: More remarkable than the modest changes in tcf and otx gene expression was the finding that RT-qPCR showed very reduced expression of eye field genes in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos (Figure 2A; rx3 reduced to 26 ± 1%, p=0.0002 and six3b reduced to 44 ± 5%, p=0.0091 of wildtype levels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1A.

claims.claim: rx3-/- mutant embryos lack eyes due to impaired specification/evagination of the optic vesicles.
claims.source: Consequently, the presence of overtly normal looking eyes in both Ztcf7l1a-/- and MZtcf7l1a-/- embryos is surprising given that rx3-/- mutant embryos lack eyes due to impaired specification/evagination of the optic vesicles (Loosli et al., 2003; Stigloher et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Loosli et al., 2003; Stigloher et al., 2006).

claims.claim: Expression of six3b and rx3 is reduced in the anterior neural plate in Ztcf7l1a-/- and tcf7l1a morphant embryos.
claims.source: We confirmed that expression of six3b and rx3 is reduced in the anterior neural plate by in situ hybridisation in Ztcf7l1a-/- and tcf7l1a morphant embryos (100%,n > 40; Figure 2F–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B; similar changes seen in MZtcf7l1a-/- mutants, data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 2F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: The expression of six3b was reduced in the eye field but not in the prechordal plate of Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants.
claims.source: The expression of six3b was reduced in the eye field but not in the prechordal plate of Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants, likely explaining why RT-qPCR showed a greater reduction in rx3 than six3b expression (Figure 2F–I; Supplementary file 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claims.claim: Analysis of eye field volume by fluorescent in situ hybridisation of rx3 revealed a reduction to 54.7% of wildtype size.
claims.source: Analysis of eye field volume by fluorescent in situ hybridisation of rx3 revealed a reduction to 54.7% of wildtype size (n = 10, Figure 2C,J–M; Supplementary file 1C) and intensity of expression within the reduced eye field also appeared reduced (Figure 2H,I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 1C, and by fluorescent in situ hybridisation images in Figure 2J-M.

claims.claim: Intensity of rx3 expression within the reduced eye field appeared reduced in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: Analysis of eye field volume by fluorescent in situ hybridisation of rx3 revealed a reduction to 54.7% of wildtype size (n = 10, Figure 2C,J–M; Supplementary file 1C) and intensity of expression within the reduced eye field also appeared reduced (Figure 2H,I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation images shown in Figure 2H,I.

claims.claim: It is the caudal region of the eye field that is most affected in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants.
claims.source: Further in situ hybridasation analysis suggests that it is the caudal region of the eye field that is most affected in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from in situ hybridisation data showing that emx3 expression rostral to the eye field is slightly broader but does not encroach into the reduced eye field, while barhl2 expression caudal to the eye field is expanded rostrally (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claims.claim: emx3 expression directly rostral to the eye field was slightly broader in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants than wildtypes but expression did not encroach into the reduced eye field.
claims.source: emx3 expression directly rostral to the eye field was slightly broader in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants than wildtypes but expression did not encroach into the reduced eye field (Figure 2D,E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, n = 5 each condition).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Expression of the prospective diencephalic marker barhl2 caudal to the reduced eye field was expanded rostrally at 10hpf in tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: Conversely, expression of the prospective diencephalic marker barhl2 caudal to the reduced eye field was expanded rostrally at 10hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D n = 5 each condition) and even more evidently at 9hpf (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E,F, 13/13 Ztcf7l1a-/-).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-F.

claims.claim: These observations suggest a caudalisation of the anterior neural plate in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants leading to reduced eye field specification.
claims.source: These observations suggest a caudalisation of the anterior neural plate in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants leading to reduced eye field specification consistent with phenotypes observed in conditions in which Wnt pathway repression is reduced (Heisenberg et al., 2001; van de Water et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the in situ hybridisation data showing rostral expansion of barhl2 and is supported by citations to previous studies (Heisenberg et al., 2001; van de Water et al., 2001).

claims.claim: RNAseq analysis of wildtype, Ztcf7l1a-/- and Ztcf7l1a-/-/Ztcf7l1b+/- embryos at 8.5hpf confirmed and extended RT-qPCR and in situ hybridisation analyses.
claims.source: RNAseq analysis of wildtype, Ztcf7l1a-/- and Ztcf7l1a-/-/Ztcf7l1b+/- embryos at 8.5hpf (80–90% epiboly stage), when the eye field is first specified confirmed and extended RT-qPCR and in situ hybridisation analyses (Supplementary file 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Supplementary file 1D.

claims.claim: In Ztcf7l1a-/-, hesx1, rx3, tcf7l1a, and fezf2 which are expressed in the prospective forebrain/eyefield were downregulated.
claims.source: In Ztcf7l1a-/-, hesx1 (Kazanskaya et al., 1997), rx3, tcf7l1a, and fezf2 (Sun et al., 2006) which are expressed in the prospective forebrain/eyefield were downregulated, whereas her5 and irx1b which are expressed more caudally in the neural plate (Müller et al., 1996, Wang et al., 2001b) were upregulated consistent with mild caudalisation of the neural plate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data (Supplementary file 1D) and citations to previous studies (Kazanskaya et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2006; Müller et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2001b).

claims.claim: her5 and irx1b which are expressed more caudally in the neural plate were upregulated in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants.
claims.source: In Ztcf7l1a-/-, hesx1 (Kazanskaya et al., 1997), rx3, tcf7l1a, and fezf2 (Sun et al., 2006) which are expressed in the prospective forebrain/eyefield were downregulated, whereas her5 and irx1b which are expressed more caudally in the neural plate (Müller et al., 1996, Wang et al., 2001b) were upregulated consistent with mild caudalisation of the neural plate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data (Supplementary file 1D) and citations to previous studies (Müller et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2001b).

claims.claim: In Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos, which do not form eyes, the expression of tcf7l1b was enhanced by about 40%.
claims.source: Additionally, in Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos, which to not form eyes, the expression of tcf7l1b was enhanced by about 40%, suggesting transcriptional compensation but evidently this was not sufficient to rescue eye formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data (Supplementary file 1D).

claims.claim: The enhanced expression of tcf7l1b in Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos suggests transcriptional compensation but this was not sufficient to rescue eye formation.
claims.source: Additionally, in Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos, which to not form eyes, the expression of tcf7l1b was enhanced by about 40%, suggesting transcriptional compensation but evidently this was not sufficient to rescue eye formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that tcf7l1b expression is enhanced but eyes still do not form in Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos.

claims.claim: Optic vesicles appear to evaginate normally in tcf7l1a-/- mutants despite the small size of eye field.
claims.source: Despite the small size of eye field in tcf7l1a-/- mutants, optic vesicles appear to evaginate normally.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time lapse analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Time lapse analysis showed that optic vesicle morphogenesis in Ztcf7l1a-/- embryos proceeded as in heterozygous sibling embryos.
claims.source: Time lapse analysis of optic vesicle evagination using the Tg(rx3:GFP)zf460Tg transgene to visualise eye field cells (Brown et al., 2010) showed that optic vesicle morphogenesis in Ztcf7l1a-/- embryos proceeded as in heterozygous sibling embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B; tcf7l1a+/-, n = 6 and Ztcf7l1a-/- n = 6; Video 1 and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B and Videos 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Transplants of wildtype cells to MZtcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos led to the recovery of rx3 expression exclusively restricted to the wildtype GFP+ cell clones.
claims.source: Transplants of wildtype cells to MZtcf7l1a-/- mutant embryos led to the recovery of rx3 expression exclusively restricted to the wildtype GFP+ cell clones (13/13 transplants, Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell transplantation data shown in Figure 3A-C (13/13 transplants).

claims.claim: The border of the GFP+ wildtype clones showed less rx3 expression, suggesting that cells at the edge of the graft are subject to cell non-autonomous signalling effects from cells surrounding the clone.
claims.source: However, the border of the GFP+ wildtype clones showed less rx3 expression, suggesting that cells at the edge of the graft are subject to cell non-autonomous signalling effects from cells surrounding the clone.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that rx3 expression is reduced at the border of wildtype cell clones in mutant hosts (Figure 3A-C).

claims.claim: MZtcf7l1a-/- mutant GFP+ cells expressed much lower levels of rx3 than wildtype neighbours when positioned in the eye field of wildtype embryos.
claims.source: Conversely, MZtcf7l1a-/- mutant GFP+ cells expressed much lower levels of rx3 than wildtype neighbours when positioned in the eye field of wildtype embryos (9/9 transplants, Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell transplantation data shown in Figure 3D-F (9/9 transplants).

claims.claim: The reduction in rx3 expression was limited to the MZtcf7l1a-/- GFP+ mutant cells.
claims.source: The reduction in rx3 expression was limited to the MZtcf7l1a-/- GFP+ mutant cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell transplantation data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the Wnt inhibitor Dkk1 expanded the anterior neural plate in both wildtype and tcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: Consistent with a cell autonomous role for Tcf7l1a in eye formation, overexpression of the Wnt inhibitor Dkk1 (Hashimoto et al., 2000) expanded the anterior neural plate in both wildtype and tcf7l1a mutants, but rx3 expression and eye field size remained much smaller in the enlarged anterior plate of tcf7l1a mutants (Figure 3G–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 3G-J and citation to Hashimoto et al., 2000.

claims.claim: rx3 expression and eye field size remained much smaller in the enlarged anterior plate of tcf7l1a mutants after Dkk1 overexpression.
claims.source: Consistent with a cell autonomous role for Tcf7l1a in eye formation, overexpression of the Wnt inhibitor Dkk1 (Hashimoto et al., 2000) expanded the anterior neural plate in both wildtype and tcf7l1a mutants, but rx3 expression and eye field size remained much smaller in the enlarged anterior plate of tcf7l1a mutants (Figure 3G–J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridisation data shown in Figure 3G-J.

claims.claim: Tcf7l1a has a cell-autonomous role in promoting eye field specification.
claims.source: All together, these results support a cell-autonomous role for Tcf7l1a in promoting eye field specification.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell transplantation experiments (Figure 3A-F) and Dkk1 overexpression experiments (Figure 3G-J).

claims.claim: Eyes in Ztcf7l1a-/- fry and adults seem indistinguishable from those in wildtype siblings.
claims.source: Despite a much-reduced eye field, eyes in Ztcf7l1a-/- fry and adults seem indistinguishable from those in wildtype siblings.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by visual observation and optokinetic response data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Optokinetic responses of Ztcf7l1a-/- and wildtype 5dpf larvae showed no significant differences at any of the four tested spatial frequencies.
claims.source: Indeed, optokinetic responses of Ztcf7l1a-/- and wildtype 5dpf larvae showed no significant differences at any of the four tested spatial frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1E), suggesting that by this stage, Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes are functional and have visual acuity comparable to that of wildtype siblings.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by optokinetic response data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1E.

claims.claim: By 5dpf, Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes are functional and have visual acuity comparable to that of wildtype siblings.
claims.source: Indeed, optokinetic responses of Ztcf7l1a-/- and wildtype 5dpf larvae showed no significant differences at any of the four tested spatial frequencies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1E), suggesting that by this stage, Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes are functional and have visual acuity comparable to that of wildtype siblings.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the optokinetic response data showing no significant differences between wildtype and mutant larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: At 24hpf, eye volume in tcf7l1a mutants was about 57% of the estimated volume of wildtype eyes at the same stage.
claims.source: At 24hpf, eye volume in mutants was about 57% of the estimated volume of wildtype eyes at the same stage (Figure 4A,C,H; Supplementary file 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by eye volume quantification data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1F.

claims.claim: By 48hpf mutant eyes were about 85% of the size of eyes in wildtype/heterozygous siblings.
claims.source: However, by 48hpf mutant eyes were about 85% of the size of eyes in wildtype/heterozygous siblings (Figure 4A,G,L; Supplementary file 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by eye volume quantification data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1F.

claims.claim: Ztcf7l1a-/- eye size did not further recover beyond 48hpf and up to 5dpf.
claims.source: Ztcf7l1a-/- eye size did not further recover beyond this time point and up to 5dpf (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B showing the ratio of Ztcf7l1a-/- to wildtype eye volume plateaus after 48hpf.

claims.claim: Eye growth in both wildtypes and Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants showed similar growth kinetics.
claims.source: Eye growth in both wildtypes and Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants showed similar growth kinetics (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth kinetics data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes follow a comparable developmental time-course as wildtype eyes in the early growth phase between 24 and 36hpf but with about 8 hr delay.
claims.source: This suggests that even though Ztcf7l1a-/-eyes are smaller, they follow a comparable developmental time-course as wildtype eyes in the early growth phase between 24 and 36hpf but with about 8 hr delay (for instance, a 32hpf Ztcf7l1a-/- eye is about the same size as a wild-type 24hpf eye).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the growth kinetics data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The temporal shift in eye growth in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants is not explained by an overall developmental delay.
claims.source: The temporal shift in eye growth in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants is not explained by an overall developmental delay as the position of the posterior lateral line primordium (pLLP) was similar to wildtype at all stages tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing similar pLLP position in wildtype and mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1G).

claims.claim: Volumes of eye cells in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants and siblings were not significantly different at 24 or 36hpf.
claims.source: Volumes of eye cells in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants and siblings were not significantly different at 24 or 36hpf and consequently cell size changes likely play no role in eye size compensation in Ztcf7l1a mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell volume quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1H.

claims.claim: Cell size changes likely play no role in eye size compensation in Ztcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: Volumes of eye cells in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants and siblings were not significantly different at 24 or 36hpf and consequently cell size changes likely play no role in eye size compensation in Ztcf7l1a mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1H).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cell volumes are not significantly different between wildtype and mutants.

claims.claim: At 36hpf, there was still a clear size difference between the experimental and control eyes after partial ablation of the optic vesicle.
claims.source: At 36hpf, there was still a clear size difference between the experimental and control eyes (Figure 4N, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4N and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and quantification data in Supplementary file 1I.

claims.claim: By 4dpf there was little or no size difference between control and experimental eyes after partial ablation of the optic vesicle.
claims.source: However, by 4dpf we observed little or no size difference between control and experimental eyes (three independent experiments, n=20/20, Figure 4O, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4O and Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and quantification data in Supplementary file 1I (n=20/20).

claims.claim: Three eyes from partially ablated optic vesicles which were ~90% the size of their control contralateral eyes at 30hpf, recovered to 100% by 3dpf.
claims.source: Three eyes from partially ablated optic vesicles which were ~90% the size of their control contralateral eyes at 30hpf, recovered to 100% by 3dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 4K, Supplementary file 1I) and five eyes which were between ~65 and~75% of control size at 30hpf recovered to 90% by 3dpf with little or no further recovery by 4dpf (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–I,K, Supplementary file 1I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4K and Supplementary file 1I.

claims.claim: The forming eye can effectively recover from either genetic or physical reduction in the size of the eye field/evaginating optic vesicle.
claims.source: Consequently, the forming eye can effectively recover from either genetic or physical reduction in the size of the eye field/evaginating optic vesicle.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from data showing size recovery in both tcf7l1a mutants and after physical ablation of optic vesicle cells.

claims.claim: Retinal neurogenesis might be delayed in Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes to extend the period of proliferative growth prior to retinal precursors undergoing neurogenic divisions.
claims.source: The observation that wildtype and Ztcf7l1a-/- mutant eyes display similar, but temporally offset, growth kinetics led us to speculate that that retinal neurogenesis might be delayed in Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes to extend the period of proliferative growth prior to retinal precursors undergoing neurogenic divisions.
claims.evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observation of similar but temporally offset growth kinetics.

claims.claim: In the zebrafish eye, neurogenesis can be visualised by tracking expression of atoh7 starting in the ventronasal retina at ~28 hpf and spreading clockwise across the central retina until it reaches the ventrotemporal side.
claims.source: In the zebrafish eye, neurogenesis can be visualised by tracking expression of atoh7 (ath5) in retinal neurons starting in the ventronasal retina at ~28 hpf and spreading clockwise across the central retina until it reaches the ventrotemporal side (Masai et al., 2000; Hu and Easter, 1999; Figure 5A–E,Q, Supplementary file 1J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Masai et al., 2000; Hu and Easter, 1999) and by data shown in Figure 5A-E,Q and Supplementary file 1J.

claims.claim: atoh7 was induced at a similar time in Ztcf7l1a-/- as in wildtype eyes.
claims.source: Although atoh7 was induced at a similar time in Ztcf7l1a-/- as in wildtype eyes, the subsequent progression of expression was delayed (Figure 5F–J,Q; Supplementary file 1J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5F-J,Q and Supplementary file 1J.

claims.claim: The subsequent progression of atoh7 expression was delayed in Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes.
claims.source: Although atoh7 was induced at a similar time in Ztcf7l1a-/- as in wildtype eyes, the subsequent progression of expression was delayed (Figure 5F–J,Q; Supplementary file 1J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5F-J,Q and Supplementary file 1J.

claims.claim: Between 36 and 40hpf, Ztcf7l1a-/- retinas expressed atoh7 exclusively in the nasal half of the retina.
claims.source: Indeed, between 36 and 40hpf, Ztcf7l1a-/- retinas expressed atoh7 exclusively in the nasal half of the retina (Figure 5H,Q), a phenotype we did not see at any stage in sibling embryo eyes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5H,Q.

claims.claim: Progression of atoh7 expression and neurogenesis is delayed by about 8–12 hr in Ztcf7l1a-/- retinas compared to siblings.
claims.source: These data indicate that progression of atoh7 expression and neurogenesis is delayed by about 8–12 hr in Ztcf7l1a-/- retinas compared to siblings, a timeframe comparable to the delays seen in optic vesicle growth.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1J.

claims.claim: Eye vesicle ablated wildtype retinas showed delayed neurogenesis compared to control non-ablated contralateral eyes at 36hpf.
claims.source: In line with our results in Ztcf7l1a-/- embryos, eye vesicle ablated wildtype retinas also showed delayed neurogenesis compared to control non-ablated contralateral eyes at 36hpf (Figure 5K,L; 6/6 ablated eyes, two independent experiments).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5K,L (6/6 ablated eyes).

claims.claim: Retinal precursors in Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes remain proliferative at stages when precursors in wildtype eyes are already producing neurons.
claims.source: Our results suggest that retinal precursors in Ztcf7l1a-/- eyes remain proliferative at stages when precursors in wildtype eyes are already producing neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the delayed neurogenesis data (Figure 5) and increased proliferation data (Figure 6).

claims.claim: Heatshocking tg(hsp70:dkk1-GFP)w32 transgenic embryos at 6hpf led to eyes ~ 34% bigger than control heat-shocked embryos by 28hpf.
claims.source: Heatshocking tg(hsp70:dkk1-GFP)w32 transgenic embryos at 6hpf led to eyes ~ 34% bigger than control heat-shocked embryos by 28hpf (Figure 5M,N,R, n = 12; Supplementary file 1K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by eye size quantification data shown in Figure 5M,N,R and Supplementary file 1K.

claims.claim: After 36hpf, wildtype eyes gradually caught up in size as growth slowed in eyes in dkk1-overexpressed embryos.
claims.source: After 36hpf, wildtype eyes gradually caught up in size as growth slowed in eyes in dkk1-overexpressed embryos (Figure 5R; Supplementary file 1K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by growth kinetics data shown in Figure 5R and Supplementary file 1K.

claims.claim: Neurogenesis was prematurely triggered by 28hpf in the eyes of dkk1 overexpressing embryos.
claims.source: Neurogenesis was prematurely triggered by 28hpf in the eyes of dkk1 overexpressing embryos, with many more cells expressing atoh7 compared to eyes in heat-shocked control embryos (Figure 5M,N, n = 7 out of 9 embryos).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by atoh7 expression data shown in Figure 5M,N (n = 7 out of 9 embryos).

claims.claim: The premature neurogenesis in dkk1 overexpressing embryos is unlikely to be due to a direct effect of dkk1 overexpression on neurogenesis.
claims.source: This result is unlikely to be due to a direct effect of dkk1 overexpression on neurogenesis as premature neurogenesis was not triggered in tg(hsp70:dkk1-GFP)w32 retinas heat-shocked at 24hpf (Figure 5O,P, n = 10, 100%).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that heat shock at 24hpf does not trigger premature neurogenesis (Figure 5O,P).

claims.claim: The results support a link between eye size and the onset of neurogenesis and the size self-regulating ability of the forming eye.
claims.source: These results further support a link between eye size and the onset of neurogenesis and the size self-regulating ability of the forming eye.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observations that larger eyes show premature neurogenesis and smaller eyes show delayed neurogenesis.

claims.claim: The proportion of PH3-positive cells standardised to the total number of cells in confocal sections at 36hpf was about 20% higher in Ztcf7l1a mutants than wildtypes.
claims.source: The proportion of PH3-positive (PH3+) cells standardised to the total number of cells in confocal sections at 36hpf was about 20% higher in Ztcf7l1a mutants than wildtypes (Figure 6A,B,C, Supplementary file 1L, wildtype, n = 7; Ztcf7l1a-/-, n = 8, p=0.021, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by PH3 quantification data shown in Figure 6A,B,C and Supplementary file 1L.

claims.claim: The proportion of PH3+ cells was similar between nasal and temporal retina and similar between wildtypes and Ztcf7l1a mutants.
claims.source: The proportion of PH3+ cells was similar between nasal and temporal retina and similar between wildtypes and Ztcf7l1a mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1L).

results.result: The tcf7l1am881 allele is a fully penetrant null mutation, but MZtcf7l1a-/- embryos develop functional eyes in EKW and AB genetic backgrounds, contrasting with the originally reported eyeless phenotype. The mutation creates complete molecular penetrance with only mutant mRNA produced, and the mutant protein is non-functional.
results.evaluation: Multiple lines of evidence support this result: RT-PCR shows only mutant mRNA in homozygotes (C24), rescue experiments confirm non-functionality of mutant protein (C26-C27), 100% of MZtcf7l1a-/- embryos from six pairings developed eyes (C22), and morpholino experiments with mo2tcf7l1a support the genetic background dependency (C33-C36). The data consistently demonstrate that the mutation is null but not essential for eye formation in certain backgrounds.

results.result: Loss of tcf7l1a function does not trigger compensatory upregulation of other lef/tcf genes at neural plate stage. RT-qPCR and RNAseq data show that lef/tcf gene expression levels either remain unchanged or are reduced in Ztcf7l1a-/- mutants at 10hpf and 8.5hpf.
results.evaluation: RT-qPCR data (C39-C43) and RNAseq analysis (C61-C63) consistently show no compensatory upregulation of lef/tcf genes. The slight reduction in forebrain size (C46) provides a plausible explanation for reduced expression of some genes. Even in Ztcf7l1a-/-/tcf7l1b+/- embryos, enhanced tcf7l1b expression was insufficient to rescue eyes (C64-C65), further supporting the lack of effective compensation.

results.result: tcf7l1a mutants show severe eye field specification defects with the eye field reduced to approximately 55% of wildtype size at 10hpf, particularly affecting the caudal region. rx3 expression is reduced to 26% and six3b to 44% of wildtype levels, indicating caudalisation of the anterior neural plate.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary approaches support this result: RT-qPCR shows dramatic reduction in eye field gene expression (C49-C51), volumetric analysis confirms 54.7% reduction in eye field size (C55), and in situ hybridization demonstrates spatial changes with rostral expansion of barhl2 (C57-C59). The data consistently point to a severe early specification defect despite later eye recovery.

results.result: Tcf7l1a functions cell-autonomously to promote eye field specification. Cell transplantation experiments show that wildtype cells recover rx3 expression in mutant hosts (13/13 transplants), while mutant cells show reduced rx3 expression in wildtype hosts (9/9 transplants). Dkk1 overexpression expands the anterior neural plate but does not rescue eye field size in mutants.
results.evaluation: The cell transplantation experiments provide strong evidence for cell autonomy with 100% penetrance in both directions (C68, C70). The Dkk1 experiments (C72-C73) further support cell autonomy by showing that manipulating Wnt signaling cannot rescue the eye field defect in mutants. The observation of reduced rx3 at clone borders (C69) suggests some non-autonomous effects but does not negate the primary cell-autonomous requirement.

results.result: Despite a much-reduced eye field, tcf7l1a mutant eyes recover to approximately 85% of wildtype size by 48hpf through compensatory growth mechanisms. The recovery shows similar growth kinetics to wildtype but with an ~8 hour temporal delay. This compensatory ability is also observed when cells are physically removed from wildtype optic vesicles.
results.evaluation: The growth kinetics data (C78-C82) demonstrate clear size recovery with quantitative measurements at multiple timepoints. Optokinetic response data (C76) confirms functional recovery. The physical ablation experiments (C86-C88) provide independent validation that size compensation is a general property of eye development. Cell volume measurements (C84) rule out cell size changes as the mechanism. The temporal offset in growth (C82) and lack of general developmental delay (C83) support a specific eye-related compensation mechanism.

results.result: Neurogenesis is delayed by approximately 8-12 hours in tcf7l1a mutant eyes, with atoh7 expression progression showing temporal offset compared to wildtype. Larger eyes generated by dkk1 overexpression show premature neurogenesis, while smaller eyes from optic vesicle ablation show delayed neurogenesis, suggesting a link between eye size and neurogenesis timing.
results.evaluation: The atoh7 expression analysis (C92-C95) provides detailed temporal data showing delayed progression in mutants. The dkk1 overexpression experiments (C98-C101) and ablation experiments (C96) provide complementary evidence linking eye size to neurogenesis timing. The observation that heat shock at 24hpf does not trigger premature neurogenesis (C101) rules out direct effects of dkk1 on neurogenesis. Together, these data support a size-dependent mechanism controlling neurogenesis onset.

results.result: tcf7l1a mutant eyes show increased proliferation at 36hpf with 20% more PH3+ cells than wildtype. Critically, the percentage of PH3+ cells co-expressing atoh7:GAP-RFP is 3.6 times lower in mutants, indicating that more retinal progenitor cells remain proliferative rather than undergoing neurogenic divisions.
results.evaluation: The PH3 quantification (C103) shows statistically significant increase in proliferation (p=0.021). The atoh7:GAP-RFP co-expression analysis (C105-C107) provides strong evidence that the increased proliferation represents continued progenitor divisions rather than neurogenic divisions, with particularly striking differences in temporal retina (C107, p<0.0001). This directly supports the proposed mechanism of compensatory growth through extended proliferation.

results.result: Although tcf7l1a mutant eyes are robust to loss of Tcf7l1a function alone, they are sensitized to additional mutations. A forward genetic screen identified mutations in hesx1, cct5, and gdf6a that produce synthetically enhanced eye phenotypes when combined with tcf7l1a mutation.
results.evaluation: The forward genetic screen successfully identified three independent modifiers (C7) that show enhanced phenotypes only in combination with tcf7l1a mutation. The detailed characterization of each modifier (described in subsequent results) validates the sensitization concept. This result establishes the principle that compensatory mechanisms can be overwhelmed by additional genetic perturbations.

results.result: A deletion in hesx1 (hesx1Δex1/2) acts as a synthetic lethal modifier of tcf7l1a, with double homozygous mutants being completely eyeless while single mutants develop normal eyes. The deletion removes exons 1 and 2 and was likely pre-existing in the fish population rather than ENU-induced.
results.evaluation: The genetic mapping (C111), molecular characterization (C115, C119), and phenotypic analysis (C124-C125) provide comprehensive evidence for the hesx1/tcf7l1a interaction. The genotyping of 53 embryos (C125) confirms the genetic interaction. The finding of the same deletion in non-mutagenized fish (C123) and the unusual nature of deletions from ENU (C116, C121) support the conclusion about its origin. This represents a clear example of synthetic lethality in eye development.

results.result: The cct5U762 mutation compromises eye growth recovery in tcf7l1a mutants. Double cct5/tcf7l1a mutant eyes fail to grow beyond 36hpf despite showing 48% increased proliferation. The phenotype is not rescued by blocking apoptosis with tp53 morpholino, and neurogenesis is severely compromised with abnormal lamination.
results.evaluation: The molecular characterization of the cct5 mutation (C131-C135) and complementation test (C136) establish it as the causative mutation. The growth arrest phenotype (C142) is well-documented with quantitative data. The tp53 rescue experiment (C145-C146) rules out apoptosis as the primary cause. The increased proliferation without growth (C148) and abnormal neurogenesis (C149-C151) suggest a fundamental defect in cell cycle progression or cell survival independent of apoptosis. The genetic interaction with tcf7l1a is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The gdf6aU768 mutation shows synthetic interaction with tcf7l1a, with double mutants showing more severe eye field reduction (eye fields ~68% of tcf7l1a single mutant size) and failure to recover eye size at later stages. Unlike tcf7l1a single mutants where eyes recover to 85% of wildtype by 48hpf, gdf6a/tcf7l1a double mutant eyes remain small at 52hpf.
results.evaluation: The eye field volumetric analysis (C157-C158) shows additive effects on eye field specification with statistically significant reductions. The failure of size recovery (C155) contrasts with the robust recovery in tcf7l1a single mutants, demonstrating compromised compensatory mechanisms (C156). The data suggest that gdf6a function is required for the compensatory growth response, though the mechanism remains unclear since gdf6a is not expressed in the eye field.

results.result: Despite the reduced eye field size in tcf7l1a mutants, optic vesicles evaginate normally as shown by time-lapse analysis of Tg(rx3:GFP) embryos.
results.evaluation: Time-lapse imaging data from 6 mutants and 6 heterozygous siblings (C67) directly demonstrates normal optic vesicle morphogenesis. This is an important observation showing that the early specification defect does not prevent subsequent morphogenetic movements, supporting the idea that compensation occurs during growth rather than specification.

results.result: Enhanced Wnt/β-Catenin activity leads to embryos with small or no eyes, while decreased activity generates embryos with bigger forebrain and eyes. The penetrance and expressivity of eye phenotypes depends on complex genetic and environmental interactions.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to multiple previous studies (C8-C9, C19) and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide important context for understanding the tcf7l1a phenotype but are not novel findings from this study.
